# Design Specification & Content Outline
# State of Developer Ecosystem 2024: Language Trends, Satisfaction, and Strategic Shifts

---

## I. Project Information

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Project Name | case-jetbrains-devecosystem |
| Canvas Format | PPT 16:9 |
| Page Count | 6 |
| Style | C) Top Consulting (Pyramid principle, conclusion-first) |
| Target Audience | Engineering leaders, CTOs, developer experience teams |
| Usage Occasion | Technology strategy briefing, hiring priority review |
| Date | 2026-04-20 |
| Template | exhibit |
| Source | JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem Report 2024 (N=23,262) |

---

## II. Canvas Specification

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Format | Standard 16:9 |
| Dimensions | 1280 × 720 px |
| viewBox | `0 0 1280 720` |
| Page Margins | Left/Right 40px, Top 20px, Bottom 40px |
| Safe Area | x: 40–1240, y: 40–680 |
| Header Area | y=20, h=60px — key message / page title |
| Content Area | y=100, h=520px |
| Footer Area | y=660, h=60px — source, confidential label, page number |

---

## III. Visual Theme

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Style | Premium dark executive, data-forward |
| Light/Dark | Dark theme for cover/chapter/ending; white content pages |
| Tone | Authoritative, precise, conclusion-first |

### Color Scheme

| Role | HEX | Usage |
|------|-----|-------|
| Primary Dark BG | `#0D1117` | Cover, chapter, ending backgrounds |
| Content BG | `#FFFFFF` | Content slide backgrounds |
| Gradient Start | `#1E40AF` | Top bar gradient start |
| Gradient End | `#7C3AED` | Top bar gradient end |
| Gold Accent | `#D4AF37` | Dividers, Exhibit bar left decoration |
| Purple-Blue Accent | `#6366F1` | Chapter numbers, secondary accents |
| Body Black | `#111827` | Body text on light backgrounds |
| Light Gray Text | `#9CA3AF` | Subtitles, descriptions |
| Tertiary Text | `#6B7280` | Footer |
| Card Background | `#1F2937` | Dark card panels |

### Data Visualization Colors (Language Series)

| Language | HEX |
|----------|-----|
| JavaScript | `#F59E0B` (amber) |
| Python | `#3B82F6` (blue) |
| TypeScript | `#8B5CF6` (purple) |
| HTML/CSS | `#EC4899` (pink) |
| SQL | `#6B7280` (gray) |
| Java | `#EF4444` (red) |
| Go | `#10B981` (green) |
| Rust | `#F97316` (orange) |
| PHP | `#94A3B8` (slate) |
| Kotlin | `#A78BFA` (violet) |

---

## IV. Typography System

### Font Plan: P5 (English-primary)

| Role | Font | Fallback |
|------|------|----------|
| Titles | Arial | Helvetica Neue, sans-serif |
| Body | Arial | Helvetica Neue, sans-serif |
| Emphasis | Arial Black | Impact, sans-serif |

### Font Size Hierarchy (Dense content, 18px baseline)

| Level | Size | Weight | Usage |
|-------|------|--------|-------|
| H1 | 52px | Bold | Cover main title |
| H2 | 28px | Bold | Page titles |
| H3 | 22px | Bold | Section titles / Exhibit bar text |
| H4 | 16px | Bold | Card titles, legend labels |
| P (body) | 14px | Regular | Body content |
| High | 40px | Bold | Highlighted KPI numbers |
| Sub | 12px | Regular | Annotations, footnotes, footer |

---

## V. Layout Principles

### Page Structure

| Zone | y-position | Height | Content |
|------|-----------|--------|---------|
| Top gradient bar | y=0 | 6px | Blue→Purple gradient |
| Header / Exhibit bar | y=20 | 55px | Dark bar + gold left line + key message |
| Content area | y=85 | 570px | Charts, tables, body text |
| Footer | y=660 | 60px | Source, CONFIDENTIAL, page number |

### Layout Modes Used

| Mode | Slides |
|------|--------|
| Single column centered | Slide 1 (cover) |
| Full-width data table | Slide 2 (language trends) |
| Left-right split (4:6) | Slide 3 (primary language) |
| Full-width horizontal bar chart | Slide 4 (satisfaction) |
| Structured heatmap table | Slide 5 (domain) |
| 2-column cards | Slide 6 (strategic takeaways) |

### Spacing

| Element | Value |
|---------|-------|
| Card gap | 20px |
| Content block gap | 24px |
| Card padding | 20px |
| Card border radius | 6px |
| Icon-to-text gap | 10px |

---

## VI. Icon Usage Spec

**Source**: Built-in icon library (640+ icons)
**Placeholder syntax**: `{{ICON:icon-name}}`

### Approved Icon List (for this deck)

| Icon Name | Usage |
|-----------|-------|
| `chart-line` | Language trends slide |
| `chart-bar` | Satisfaction slide reference |
| `arrow-trend-up` | Growth indicators |
| `arrow-trend-down` | Decline indicators |
| `lightbulb` | Insights, takeaways |
| `target` | Strategic goals |
| `users` | Developer community |
| `rocket` | Growth languages |
| `code` | Programming language context |
| `trophy` | Top-ranked languages |
| `flag` | Strategic priorities |
| `database` | Data/analytics domain |
| `globe` | Web/UI domain |
| `server` | Systems/infra domain |

---

## VII. Chart Reference List

| Chart Type | Template Path | Used In | Purpose |
|------------|--------------|---------|---------|
| Multi-series line chart (custom) | — | Slide 2 | 8-year language usage trends 2017–2024 |
| Horizontal bar chart | `templates/charts/horizontal_bar_chart.svg` | Slide 3 | Primary language % + adoption intent |
| Horizontal bar chart | `templates/charts/horizontal_bar_chart.svg` | Slide 4 | Developer satisfaction scores top 10 |
| Custom heatmap/table | — | Slide 5 | Language-domain matrix |
| Structured card grid | — | Slide 6 | 5 strategic takeaways |

---

## VIII. Image Resource List

No external images used. All visuals are SVG-native charts and data tables.

---

## IX. Content Outline

### Slide 1 — Cover
**Type**: Cover (dark)
**Layout**: Single column centered, dark `#0D1117` background
**Title**: State of Developer Ecosystem 2024: Language Trends, Satisfaction, and Strategic Shifts
**Subtitle**: Key insights from JetBrains' survey of 23,262 developers on programming language usage, satisfaction, adoption intent, and domain specialization trends from 2017 to 2024.
**Content points**:
- Source badge: JetBrains 2024 Annual Survey · N = 23,262 developers worldwide
- Date: April 2026
- Confidential label at bottom

---

### Slide 2 — Language Trends
**Type**: Content (white background, Exhibit bar)
**Layout**: Full-width multi-series comparison table
**Title**: Python Closes the Gap: 8 Years of Language Usage Shifts
**Key message (Exhibit bar)**: JavaScript peaked at 70% in 2020 and is now declining; Python has nearly closed the gap, rising from 32% to 57%
**Content points**:
- Comparison table showing usage % for 8 languages across 4 time points (2017, 2020, 2022, 2024)
- Color-coded trend arrows per language
- Languages: JavaScript, Python, HTML/CSS, SQL, Java, TypeScript, Go, Rust, PHP, Kotlin
- Highlight rows: Python (growth), TypeScript (strong growth), PHP (significant decline)
- Data source: JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2024

**Data table**:
| Language | 2017 | 2020 | 2022 | 2024 | Trend |
|----------|------|------|------|------|-------|
| JavaScript | 65% | 70% | 65% | 61% | ↓ Declining |
| Python | 32% | 55% | 53% | 57% | ↑ Strong growth |
| HTML/CSS | 60% | 61% | 54% | 51% | ↓ Gradual decline |
| SQL | 42% | 56% | 49% | 48% | → Plateaued |
| Java | 47% | 54% | 48% | 46% | ↓ Slow decline |
| TypeScript | 12% | 28% | 34% | 37% | ↑ Tripled |
| Go | 8% | 19% | 19% | 18% | → Plateaued |
| Rust | —% | 7% | 9% | 11% | ↑ Steady growth |
| PHP | 30% | 27% | 20% | 17% | ↓ Significant decline |
| Kotlin | 2% | 17% | 16% | 14% | → Plateaued |

---

### Slide 3 — Primary Language
**Type**: Content (white, Exhibit bar)
**Layout**: Left-right split (4:6) — horizontal bar chart left, insight cards right
**Title**: Python Is Now the #1 Primary Language at 35%
**Key message (Exhibit bar)**: Developer ecosystem lock-in is strong — adoption intent stays below 6% across all languages
**Content points**:
- Left: Horizontal bar chart — Primary language (% as primary)
  - Python 35%, Java 30%, JavaScript 28%, TypeScript 19%, SQL 17%
- Right: Insight column with two contrast cards
  - Card 1: "Adoption intent stays below 6%" — contrast: primary usage vs intent
  - Card 2 (5 rows): Python 35% vs 6% intent, Java 30% vs 4%, JS 28% vs ~2%, TS 19% vs 5%, SQL 17% vs 4%
- Footer note: AI/ML boom directly drove Python to #1 primary language

---

### Slide 4 — Developer Satisfaction
**Type**: Content (white, Exhibit bar)
**Layout**: Full-width horizontal bar chart, top 10 languages
**Title**: TypeScript and Rust Top Developer Satisfaction, Nearly Tied at 199 vs 198
**Key message (Exhibit bar)**: Type-safe, modern-tooling languages dominate satisfaction — a signal for retention strategy
**Content points**:
- Horizontal bar chart: satisfaction scores, top 10
  1. TypeScript — 199
  2. Rust — 198
  3. Python — 151
  4. Go — 129
  5. Lua — 118
  6. C++ — 113
  7. Kotlin — 113
  8. Shell — 100
  9. Dart — 93
  10. C — 86
- Callout annotation: "TypeScript & Rust lead by ~30% over Python — gap reflects type safety + modern DX"
- Color-code bars by language per color scheme

---

### Slide 5 — Domain Specialization
**Type**: Content (white, Exhibit bar)
**Layout**: Structured domain-language matrix table (heatmap-style)
**Title**: Each Language Owns a Domain: AI Belongs to Python, UI to TypeScript
**Key message (Exhibit bar)**: Language choice is domain-driven, not preference-driven — hire and invest accordingly
**Content points**:
- Matrix table: Domain rows × Top Language columns
  | Domain | #1 Language | Share | #2 Language |
  |--------|------------|-------|-------------|
  | AI / Machine Learning | Python | 31% | — |
  | Data Science & Analytics | Python | 28% | SQL |
  | Data Processing | Python | 17% | — |
  | Integrating with APIs | Python | 38% | — |
  | User Interface | TypeScript | 62% | JavaScript (58%) |
  | APIs & Services | Java | 49% | — |
  | App Logic & Workflows | Java | 55% | — |
  | System Tools & Components | C++ | 27% | — |
- Color intensity on share % (deeper = higher dominance)
- Callout: Python owns 4 of 8 domains; TypeScript dominates UI at 62%

---

### Slide 6 — Strategic Takeaways
**Type**: Content (white, Exhibit bar)
**Layout**: 2×2 card grid + 1 full-width bottom card (5 takeaways total)
**Title**: What This Means for Your Technology Strategy in 2025
**Key message (Exhibit bar)**: Five actionable decisions for engineering leaders: invest, future-proof, grow, wind down, and retain
**Content points**:
- Card 1 (top-left): **Invest in Python for AI/ML** — Python leads AI (31%), data science (28%), is primary language for 35% of devs. Non-negotiable for AI-forward organizations.
- Card 2 (top-right): **TypeScript is the future of frontend & full-stack** — Tripled usage (12%→37%), #1 satisfaction, owns UI at 62%. Standardize TypeScript in web teams.
- Card 3 (bottom-left): **Rust & Go are infrastructure growth plays** — Most-adopted languages; Rust 7%→11%, Go 8%→18%. Critical for cloud-native, systems, and performance-sensitive services.
- Card 4 (bottom-right): **PHP & Ruby hiring pools are shrinking** — PHP: 30%→17%; Ruby: 10%→4% over 8 years. Factor into long-term talent planning.
- Card 5 (full-width bottom): **Satisfaction = retention lever** — TypeScript (199) and Rust (198) developers are the most engaged. Factor language choice into team happiness and attrition strategy.

---

## X. Speaker Notes Requirements

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Total Duration | 12–15 minutes |
| Notes Style | Formal / executive briefing |
| Presentation Purpose | Inform and persuade |
| File Naming | `01_cover.md`, `02_language-trends.md`, etc. in `notes/` |
| Structure per note | [Talking point] → [Data reference] → [So what] |
| Rule | No `#` heading lines in split note files |

---

## XI. Technical Constraints Reminder

1. All SVGs: `viewBox="0 0 1280 720"`, no width/height attributes
2. No `clipPath`, `mask`, `<style>`, `class`, `foreignObject`, `animate*`, `script`
3. No `rgba()` — use `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity`
4. No `<g opacity="...">` — set opacity on individual child elements
5. Text wrapping via `<tspan>` only
6. Arrows via `<polygon>` triangles, not `<marker>`
7. Gradients via `<defs><linearGradient>`
8. Inline styles only — no external CSS

---

## XII. Design Checklist

**Pre-generation**:
- [x] Eight Confirmations completed
- [x] Content outline finalized for all 6 slides
- [x] Chart types confirmed per slide
- [x] Data values verified against source_brief.md only
- [x] Icon list validated against icons_index.json
- [x] No fabricated data

**Post-generation**:
- [ ] All 6 SVGs in `svg_output/`
- [ ] Speaker notes in `notes/total.md`
- [ ] `finalize_svg.py` run
- [ ] PPTX exported from `svg_final/`

---

## XIII. Next Steps

- Card 5 (full-width bottom): **Satisfaction = retention lever** — TypeScript (199) and Rust (198) developers are the most engaged. Factor language choice into team happiness and attrition strategy.

---

## X. Speaker Notes Requirements

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Total Duration | 12–15 minutes |
| Notes Style | Formal / executive briefing |
| Presentation Purpose | Inform and persuade |
| File Naming | `01_cover.md`, `02_language-trends.md`, etc. in `notes/` |
| Structure per note | [Talking point] → [Data reference] → [So what] |
| Rule | No `#` heading lines in split note files |

---

## XI. Technical Constraints Reminder

1. All SVGs: `viewBox="0 0 1280 720"`, no width/height attributes
2. No `clipPath`, `mask`, `<style>`, `class`, `foreignObject`, `animate*`, `script`
3. No `rgba()` — use `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity`
4. No `<g opacity="...">` — set opacity on individual child elements
5. Text wrapping via `<tspan>` only
6. Arrows via `<polygon>` triangles, not `<marker>`
7. Gradients via `<defs><linearGradient>`
8. Inline styles only — no external CSS

---

## XII. Design Checklist

**Pre-generation**:
- [x] Eight Confirmations completed
- [x] Content outline finalized for all 6 slides
- [x] Chart types confirmed per slide
- [x] Data values verified against source_brief.md only
- [x] Icon list validated against icons_index.json
- [x] No fabricated data

**Post-generation**:
- [ ] All 6 SVGs in `svg_output/`
- [ ] Speaker notes in `notes/total.md`
- [ ] `finalize_svg.py` run
- [ ] PPTX exported from `svg_final/`

---

## XIII. Next Steps

No AI image generation needed (Option A — no images).

→ **Proceed directly to Executor phase (Top Consulting style)**
→ Read `references/executor-base.md` + `references/executor-consultant-top.md`
→ Generate 6 SVG pages sequentially into `svg_output/`

# Executor Common Guidelines

> Style-specific content is in the corresponding `executor-{style}.md`. Technical constraints are in shared-standards.md.

---

## 1. Template Adherence Rules

If template files exist in the project's `templates/` directory, the template structure must be followed:

| Page Type | Corresponding Template | Adherence Rules |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|
| Cover | `01_cover.svg` | Inherit background, decorative elements, layout structure; replace placeholder content |
| Chapter | `02_chapter.svg` | Inherit numbering style, title position, decorative elements |
| Content | `03_content.svg` | Inherit header/footer styles; **content area may be freely laid out** |
| Ending | `04_ending.svg` | Inherit background, thank-you message position, contact info layout |
| TOC | `02_toc.svg` | **Optional**: Inherit TOC title, list styles |

### Page-Template Mapping Declaration (Required Output)

Before generating each page, you must explicitly output which template (or "free design") is used:

```
📝 **Template mapping**: `templates/01_cover.svg` (or "None (free design)")
🎯 **Adherence rules / layout strategy**: [specific description]
```

- **Content pages**: Templates only define header and footer; the content area is freely laid out by the Executor
- **No template**: Generate entirely per the Design Specification & Content Outline

---

## 2. Design Parameter Confirmation (Mandatory Step)

> Before generating the first SVG page, you **must review the key design parameters from the Design Specification & Content Outline** to ensure all subsequent generation strictly follows the spec.

Must output confirmation including: canvas dimensions, body font size, color scheme (primary/secondary/accent HEX values), font plan.

**Why is this step mandatory?** Prevents the "spec says one thing, execution does another" disconnect.

---

## 3. Execution Guidelines

- **Proximity principle**: Place related elements close together to form visual groups; increase spacing between unrelated groups to reinforce logical structure
- **Absolute spec adherence**: Strictly follow the color, layout, canvas format, and typography parameters in the spec
- **Follow template structure**: If templates exist, inherit the template's visual framework
- **Phased batch generation** (recommended):
  1. **Visual Construction Phase**: Generate all SVG pages continuously, ensuring high consistency in design style and layout coordinates (Visual Consistency)
  2. **Logic Construction Phase**: After all SVGs are finalized, batch-generate speaker notes to ensure narrative coherence (Narrative Continuity)
- **Technical specifications**: See [shared-standards.md](shared-standards.md) for SVG technical constraints and PPT compatibility rules

### SVG File Naming Convention

File naming format: `<number>_<page_name>.svg`

- **Chinese content** → Chinese naming: `01_封面.svg`, `02_目录.svg`, `03_核心优势.svg`
- **English content** → English naming: `01_cover.svg`, `02_agenda.svg`, `03_key_benefits.svg`
- **Number rules**: Two-digit numbers, starting from 01
- **Page name**: Concise and descriptive, matching the page title in the Design Specification & Content Outline

---

## 4. Icon Usage

Four approaches: **A: Emoji** (`<text>🚀</text>`) | **B: AI-generated** (SVG basic shapes) | **C: Built-in library** (`templates/icons/` 640+ icons, recommended) | **D: Custom** (user-specified)

**Built-in icons — Placeholder method (recommended)**:

```xml
<use data-icon="chart-bar" x="100" y="200" width="48" height="48" fill="#005587"/>
```

> No need to manually run `embed_icons.py`; `finalize_svg.py` post-processing tool will auto-embed icons.

**Common icons**: `chart-bar` `arrow-trend-up` `users` `cog` `circle-checkmark` `target` `clock` `file` `dollar` `lightbulb`

> ⚠️ **Icon validation rule**: If the Design Specification includes an icon inventory list, Executor may **only** use icons from that approved list. Using icon names not in the index is FORBIDDEN — verify against `templates/icons/icons_index.json` if uncertain.

Full index: `templates/icons/README.md`

---

## 5. Chart Reference

When the Design Spec includes a **VII. Chart Reference List**, read the referenced SVG templates from `templates/charts/` to understand common chart patterns.

**Adaptation rules**:
- **Must preserve**: Chart type (bar/line/pie etc.) as specified in the Design Spec
- **Must adapt**: Data values, labels, colors (match the project's color scheme), and dimensions to fit the page layout
- **May adjust**: Axis ranges, grid lines, legend position, spacing — as long as the chart remains accurate and readable
- **Must NOT**: Change chart type without Design Spec justification, or remove data points specified in the outline

> Chart templates: `templates/charts/` (33 types). Index: `templates/charts/charts_index.json`

---

## 6. Image Handling

Handle images based on their status in the Design Specification's "Image Resource List":

| Status | Source | Handling |
|--------|--------|----------|
| **Existing** | User-provided | Reference images directly from `../images/` directory |
| **AI-generated** | Generated by Image_Generator | Images already in `../images/`, reference directly |
| **Placeholder** | Not yet prepared | Use dashed border placeholder |

**Reference**: `<image href="../images/xxx.png" ... preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>`

**Placeholder**: Dashed border `<rect stroke-dasharray="8,4" .../>` + description text

---

## 7. Font Usage

Apply corresponding fonts for different text roles based on the font plan in the Design Specification & Content Outline:

| Role | Chinese Recommended | English Recommended |
|------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Title font | Microsoft YaHei / KaiTi / SimHei | Arial / Georgia |
| Body font | Microsoft YaHei / SimSun | Calibri / Times |
| Emphasis font | SimHei | Arial Black / Consolas |
| Annotation font | Microsoft YaHei / SimSun | Arial / Times |

---

## 8. Speaker Notes Generation Framework

### Task 1. Generate Complete Speaker Notes Document

After **all SVG pages are generated and finalized**, enter the "Logic Construction Phase" and generate the complete speaker notes document in `notes/total.md`.

**Why not generate page-by-page?** Batch-writing notes allows planning transitions like a script, ensuring coherent presentation logic.

**Format**: Each page starts with `# <number>_<page_title>`, separated by `---` between pages. Each page includes: script text (2-5 sentences), `Key points: ① ② ③`, `Duration: X minutes`. Except for the first page, each page's text starts with a `[Transition]` phrase.

**Basic stage direction markers** (common to all styles):

| Marker | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `[Pause]` | Whitespace after key content, letting the audience absorb |
| `[Transition]` | Standalone paragraph at the start of each page's text, bridging from the previous page |

> Each style may extend with additional markers (`[Interactive]`/`[Data]`/`[Scan Room]`/`[Benchmark]` etc.), see `executor-{style}.md`.

**Requirements**:

- Notes should be conversational and flow naturally
- Highlight each page's core information and presentation key points
- Users can manually edit and override in the `notes/` directory

### Task 2. Split Into Per-Page Note Files

Automatically split `notes/total.md` into individual speaker note files in the `notes/` directory.

**File naming convention**:

- **Recommended**: Match SVG names (e.g., `01_cover.svg` → `notes/01_cover.md`)

74	|-------|----------|-----------|
75	| Core conclusion | Takeaway Box | 16-18px bold |
76	| Arguments | Content area body | 14-16px |
77	| Supporting data | Charts / cards | 12-14px |
78	
79	**Contrast**: Title "Market Research Results" (wrong) → "Metaverse needs 5-10 years to reach scale" (right); Body "We researched... and found..." (wrong) → "Three arguments: (1)... (2)... (3)..." (right)
80	
81	---
82	
83	## MBB-level Layout Patterns
84	
85	### Content Page Standard Structure (1280x720)
86	
87	```
88	┌──────────────────────────────────┐
89	│ Gradient top bar (0,0 → 1280,6)  │
90	├──────────────────────────────────┤
91	│ Assertion title (x=40, y=50, 24px)│
92	├──────────────────────────────────┤
93	│ Takeaway Box (x=40, y=75,        │  ← Dark background + white text, one-sentence conclusion
94	│   w=1200, h=45)                  │
95	├──────────────────────────────────┤
96	│ Content area (x=40, y=140,       │  ← Charts / data / analysis
97	│   w=1200, h=520)                 │
98	├──────────────────────────────────┤
99	│ Source | CONFIDENTIAL | Page #    │  ← y=700, 10px
100	└──────────────────────────────────┘
101	```
102	
103	### Strategic Roadmap
104	
105	Three phases laid out horizontally, `<rect rx="8">` + title + action list, `<polygon>` arrows connecting:
106	
107	```
108	Focus Core (0-6mo)  ──>  Expand Capability (6-12mo)  ──>  Scale Up (12-18mo)
109	x=40,w=380              x=450,w=380                     x=860,w=380
110	```
111	
112	### Benchmarking Matrix
113	
114	Horizontal table; own row highlighted in theme color, others in gray. Leading indicators marked green, lagging marked red. Use `<circle>` or `<rect>` to build score points.
115	
116	### Waterfall Chart (Change Attribution)
117	
118	Start → increase/decrease factors → End. Positive factors green bars, negative factors red bars, start/end points dark bars, cumulative line as dashed connector.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## Strategic Use of Color
123	
124	MBB-level color usage is extremely restrained — color serves information:
125	
126	| Purpose | Method |
127	|---------|--------|
128	| **Focus** | Target data in theme color, everything else gray |
129	| **Reduce cognitive load** | Same series differentiated by opacity (`fill-opacity` 1.0/0.6/0.3) |
130	| **Semantics** | Green = positive, Red = negative, Gray = baseline |
131	| **Branding** | Gradient top bar / decorative lines in brand color |
132	
133	**Commandments**: No more than 3 primary colors; accent color used at most 2-3 places globally; data series use same-hue depth variations, not different colors; background white or very light gray.
134	
135	---
136	
137	## Chart vs Table Selection Matrix
138	
139	| Scenario | Recommended Form | Reason |
140	|----------|-----------------|--------|
141	| Comparing 2-7 categories | **Bar chart** | Visual comparison is intuitive |
142	| Time trends | **Line chart** | Time series clarity |
143	| Precise values / large rankings | **Table** | 50 data points in a bar chart would be chaotic |
144	| Proportional composition | **Donut chart** | More modern than pie charts |
145	| Two-dimensional positioning | **2x2 matrix** | Strategic quadrant analysis |
146	| Change attribution | **Waterfall chart** | Factor decomposition |
147	
148	---
149	
150	## Speaker Notes Style
151	
152	### Narrative Tone
153	
154	Targeting **executives / decision-makers**. Pyramid structure — every sentence carries information. Composed, authoritative, and insightful tone.
155	
156	### Stage Direction Markers
157	
158	| Marker | Purpose | Example |
159	|--------|---------|---------|
160	| `[Pause]` | Silence after key insight, let executives absorb | "This means we are missing a billion-dollar market. [Pause]" |
161	| `[Scan Room]` | Observe decision-makers' reactions, decide whether to elaborate | "[Scan Room] If there are questions, I can elaborate." |
162	| `[Data]` | Conversational number delivery | "[Data] 63% → nearly two-thirds" |
163	| `[Benchmark]` | Emphasize comparison baseline | "[Benchmark] Compared to the industry average of 12%, our 23% is nearly double" |
164	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Building on the strategic framework, let's drill into the implementation path." |
165	
166	### Notes Writing Guidelines
167	
168	- **Pyramid structure**: Conclusion → Arguments → Details
169	- **Data contextualization**: Every number has a comparison reference
170	- **Executive language**: "The strategic implication is...", "The core insight is..."
171	- **Flex mechanism**: Annotate "content that can be skipped if time is tight" for flexible duration
172	- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core insight (2) Data support (3) Strategic implication`
173	
174	### Notes Example
175	
176	```markdown
177	# 03_strategic_path
178	
179	[Transition] Having clarified the problem and the opportunity, now comes the most critical part — our response path.
180	
181	We recommend a three-phase strategy. [Pause]
182	
183	Phase one: Focus. Over the next six months, concentrate resources on conquering the Eastern China market.
184	[Data] Eastern China contributes nearly two-thirds of industry growth, [Benchmark] yet our penetration rate is only half of Competitor A's. [Pause]
185	
186	Phase two: Expand. Use Eastern China as a template, replicate to Southern and Northern China.
187	Phase three: Scale. Leverage a digital platform for nationwide coverage.
188	
189	[Scan Room] The resource allocation for phase one is in the appendix — would you like me to walk through it now?
190	
191	Key points: (1) Focus-Expand-Scale three-phase approach (2) Data-backed Eastern China priority (3) 18-month full deployment
192	Duration: 3 minutes
193	Flex: [If time is tight, skip phase two and three details and go straight to financial impact]
194	```
195	
196	---
197	
198	## MBB-level Quality Checklist Supplement
199	
200	### Content Level
201	
202	- [ ] **SCQA complete**: Overall follows Situation-Complication-Question-Answer structure
203	- [ ] **Data contextualized**: Every data point has a comparison reference
204	- [ ] **Conclusion first**: Every page's Takeaway Box has a one-sentence conclusion
205	- [ ] **MECE principle**: Categorized analysis is mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
206	
207	### Visual Level
208	
209	- [ ] **Color with intent**: Colors serve information delivery
210	- [ ] **Ample whitespace**: Not crowded; information can "breathe"
211	- [ ] **Visual hierarchy**: Conclusion > Arguments > Details, differentiated by font size/weight
212	- [ ] **Brand consistency**: Gradient top bar and footer unified throughout
213	
214	### Notes Level
215	
216	- [ ] **Pyramid structure**: Every page is conclusion-first
217	- [ ] **Stage markers complete**: [Pause] and [Scan Room] at key positions
218	- [ ] **Flex content annotated**: Supports flexible duration
219

  <text x="58" y="52" fill="#FFFFFF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold">Five decisions for 2025: invest in Python, standardize TypeScript, bet on Rust/Go for infra, wind down PHP/Ruby, use language satisfaction as a retention lever</text>

  <!-- Page title -->
  <text x="40" y="90" fill="#111827" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="22" font-weight="bold">What This Means for Your Technology Strategy in 2025</text>

  <rect x="40" y="104" width="590" height="210" fill="#EFF6FF" rx="6"/>

  <text x="58" y="150" fill="#111827" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold">Invest in Python for AI/ML Teams</text>
  <rect x="58" y="162" width="550" height="1" fill="#BFDBFE"/>
  <text x="58" y="182" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">Python leads AI/ML (31%), data science (28%), and API</text>
  <text x="58" y="199" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">integration (38%). It is now the #1 primary language at 35%</text>
  <text x="58" y="216" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">of developers — driven by the AI boom.</text>
  <rect x="58" y="232" width="200" height="26" fill="#3B82F6" rx="4"/>
  <text x="158" y="249" text-anchor="middle" fill="#FFFFFF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Non-negotiable for AI orgs</text>
  <use data-icon="rocket" x="570" y="152" width="32" height="32" fill="#3B82F6"/>

  <text x="668" y="199" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">development at 62%. Tied #1 in satisfaction at score 199 —</text>
  <text x="668" y="216" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">developers love it and adopt it rapidly.</text>

  <use data-icon="arrow-trend-up" x="1180" y="152" width="32" height="32" fill="#8B5CF6"/>

  <rect x="40" y="328" width="4" height="210" fill="#10B981" rx="2"/>

  <rect x="58" y="386" width="550" height="1" fill="#A7F3D0"/>
  <text x="58" y="406" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">Most-planned-to-adopt languages. Go: 8%→18% (2017–2024),</text>
  <text x="58" y="423" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">stabilized for cloud-native. Rust: effectively 0%→11%, still</text>
  <text x="58" y="440" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">climbing for systems, infra, and performance-critical services.</text>
  <rect x="58" y="456" width="260" height="26" fill="#10B981" rx="4"/>
  <text x="188" y="473" text-anchor="middle" fill="#FFFFFF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Hire Rust/Go for infra & platform teams</text>
  <use data-icon="server" x="570" y="376" width="32" height="32" fill="#10B981"/>

  <!-- Card 4: PHP/Ruby declining (bottom-right) -->
  <rect x="650" y="328" width="590" height="210" fill="#FEF2F2" rx="6"/>
  <rect x="650" y="328" width="590" height="6" fill="#EF4444" rx="3"/>
  <rect x="650" y="328" width="4" height="210" fill="#EF4444" rx="2"/>
  <text x="668" y="351" fill="#B91C1C" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" letter-spacing="1">DECISION 04</text>
  <text x="668" y="374" fill="#111827" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="17" font-weight="bold">PHP & Ruby Hiring Pools Are Shrinking</text>
  <rect x="668" y="386" width="550" height="1" fill="#FECACA"/>
  <text x="668" y="406" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">PHP dropped from 30% to 17% over 8 years (–43%). Ruby</text>
  <text x="668" y="423" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">fell from 10% to 4%. New developer talent is choosing</text>
  <text x="668" y="440" fill="#374151" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">Python and TypeScript instead.</text>
  <rect x="668" y="456" width="270" height="26" fill="#EF4444" rx="4"/>
  <text x="803" y="473" text-anchor="middle" fill="#FFFFFF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" font-weight="bold">Factor into long-term talent planning</text>
  <use data-icon="arrow-trend-down" x="1180" y="376" width="32" height="32" fill="#EF4444"/>

  <!-- Card 5: Full-width retention -->
  <rect x="40" y="552" width="1200" height="84" fill="#0D1117" rx="6"/>
  <rect x="40" y="552" width="1200" height="5" fill="url(#top-gradient)" rx="3"/>
  <rect x="40" y="552" width="5" height="84" fill="#D4AF37" rx="2"/>
  <text x="60" y="574" fill="#D4AF37" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" letter-spacing="1">DECISION 05 — RETENTION LEVER</text>
  <text x="60" y="597" fill="#FFFFFF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold">Satisfaction = Retention: TypeScript (199) & Rust (198) developers are the most engaged</text>
  <text x="60" y="619" fill="#9CA3AF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13">Language choice directly impacts developer happiness. Giving engineers access to modern, type-safe languages reduces attrition risk. Factor this into stack decisions.</text>
  <use data-icon="trophy" x="1192" y="572" width="36" height="36" fill="#D4AF37"/>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <rect x="40" y="660" width="1200" height="1" fill="#E5E7EB"/>
  <text x="40" y="685" fill="#9CA3AF" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10">Source: JetBrains Developer Ecosystem Survey 2024 · N=23,262</text>
  <text x="640" y="685" text-anchor="middle" fill="#D4AF37" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="10">CONFIDENTIAL</text>
  <text x="1240" y="685" text-anchor="end" fill="#6B7280" font-family="Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11">6 / 6</text>

# 01_cover

[Transition] Welcome. This briefing draws on the JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem 2024 survey — the most comprehensive annual snapshot of the global developer community.

The data behind this deck comes from 23,262 developers worldwide, tracked across 20 programming languages over eight consecutive years from 2017 to 2024. This is not anecdotal — it is a statistically robust signal of where the industry is heading.

[Pause] Over the next 12 minutes, we will cover three questions: which languages are gaining and losing ground, where developer satisfaction is highest, and what that means for your technology investments and hiring priorities.

Key points: (1) Source: JetBrains 2024 survey, N=23,262 (2) Eight-year longitudinal dataset (3) Structured around three strategic questions
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_language_trends

[Transition] Let's begin with the macro picture — how the language landscape has shifted over the past eight years.

The headline is clear: JavaScript is still the most widely used language at 61%, but it peaked at 70% in 2020 and has been declining since. Meanwhile, Python has risen from 32% to 57% — nearly closing the gap entirely.

[Data] TypeScript has tripled its usage share — from 12% in 2017 to 37% in 2024. That is not a modest uptick; that is a structural shift toward typed, modern development.

[Benchmark] On the other end, PHP dropped from 30% to 17% — a 43% relative decline in eight years. Ruby fell similarly. These are not temporary dips — they are ecosystem contractions.

[Pause]

Key points: (1) Python nearly matches JavaScript at 57% vs 61% (2) TypeScript tripled — strongest growth of any major language (3) PHP and Ruby in structural long-term decline
Duration: 2.5 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, focus on Python growth and PHP decline; skip Go/Kotlin details]

---

# 03_primary_language

[Transition] Usage rates tell us who is using a language. But the primary language question tells us something more important — which language engineers have made their core identity.

Python is now the #1 primary language for 35% of developers, ahead of Java at 30% and JavaScript at 28%. This is a significant shift from prior years when Java dominated enterprise teams.

[Data] Here is what makes this strategically important: adoption intent is below 6% across all languages. [Pause] Developers are not planning to switch stacks. The lock-in effect is real.

[Benchmark] This means: if Python is not already your primary language for AI and data work, you cannot quickly retrain your way to it. You need to hire or invest in structured upskilling — the market will not self-correct.

Key points: (1) Python overtakes Java as #1 primary language (2) Adoption intent below 6% = strong ecosystem lock-in (3) Strategic implication: hire Python talent now, do not wait
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_developer_satisfaction

[Transition] Usage tells us what developers do. Satisfaction tells us what developers love — and love is what drives retention and productivity.

TypeScript and Rust sit virtually tied at the top — 199 and 198 respectively. They lead Python, the third-place language, by 48 satisfaction points. [Pause]

[Benchmark] That gap is not coincidental. TypeScript and Rust share a common trait: strong type systems and modern developer tooling. The pattern is clear — developers feel most productive and engaged when the language helps them catch errors early and ship with confidence.

[Scan Room] The retention implication here is direct: if you are asking engineers to work primarily in languages that score lower on satisfaction — say, C at 86 or PHP — you are creating an avoidable attrition risk.

Key points: (1) TypeScript 199, Rust 198 — nearly tied at #1 and #2 (2) Type-safety and modern tooling are the common denominator (3) Satisfaction gap is a retention signal — factor into stack decisions
Duration: 2.5 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, focus on top 3: TypeScript, Rust, Python]

---

# 05_domain_specialization

[Transition] Having seen what developers prefer globally, let us look at where each language actually dominates — the application domains.

The data is unambiguous: language choice follows domain, not personal preference. Python owns three of the seven domains we tracked. It leads AI and machine learning at 31%, data science at 28%, and API integration at 38%.

[Data] TypeScript commands user interface development at 62% — that is nearly two-thirds of frontend developers. Java holds enterprise firmly at 49% for APIs and services and 55% for application logic. C++ still leads systems tooling at 27%.

[Benchmark] The strategic implication: if you are building AI capabilities, you need Python. If you are building web products, you need TypeScript. If you are building infrastructure, Go and Rust are the growth languages. There is no universal language — but there are wrong choices for each domain.

Key points: (1) Python owns AI/ML, data, and integration (2) TypeScript owns UI at 62% (3) Java still dominates enterprise services; C++ leads systems
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 06_strategic_takeaways

[Transition] Let me bring this together into five decisions you can act on.

First: invest in Python for AI/ML. It is the undisputed language of data science and artificial intelligence — 31% in AI, 28% in data science, #1 primary language overall. This is not a trend; it is a settled fact.

Second: standardize TypeScript across your web teams. Usage tripled over eight years. It tops satisfaction. It owns frontend at 62%. The business case for TypeScript migration is stronger now than it has ever been.

Third: treat Rust and Go as your infrastructure growth plays. These are the two most planned-to-adopt languages. For cloud-native, platform, and systems work, they deliver what modern infrastructure demands: performance, safety, and concurrency.

[Pause]

Fourth: factor PHP and Ruby into your talent planning. Their hiring pools are contracting — down 43% and 60% respectively. Long-term dependency on these stacks creates recruiting risk.

Fifth, and perhaps most actionable: use language satisfaction as a retention lever. TypeScript and Rust developers score 199 and 198. If your engineers are working in languages they dislike, you are losing them silently. Modernize the stack — it pays back in engagement.

[Scan Room] I am happy to go deeper on any of these five decisions, or we can open it up for questions.

Key points: (1) Python=AI/ML investment; TypeScript=frontend standard; Rust/Go=infra (2) PHP/Ruby pools shrinking — plan accordingly (3) Satisfaction correlates with retention — language choice is a talent strategy
Duration: 2.5 minutes
